messages.subject: [statnet_help] Unbalanced sample size for testing homophily effect
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Unbalanced sample size for testing homophily effect
messages.body_plain:
Dear folks,

I have several classroom directed friendship network data collected by classroom roster. I want to try to test the gender homophily within each classroom. But the number of students from each gender is not balanced in some classrooms, for example, 4 boys and 21 girls in a class.

 I am wondering whether such unbalanced sample size of each gender will lead to incorrect results via nodematch()? How could I solve this problem if unbalanced sample size matters?

By the way, how shall I interpret results from different classroom networks (i.e. how shall I "generalize" a result from homophily tests of different classrooms)?

Thanks for your kind help in advance and all the best for the new year!

Best,
Shupin

messages.body_plain:
Shupin,

As long as you include a main effect for sex (nodefactor(sex)) in the 
model, this should control for the composition differences and give you an 
estimate for the homophily term that can be compared across classrooms.

But note that with only 4 boys in a classroom, there is not much 
information that can be obtained, and I would expect the se's to be large 
in that case.

hth,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I used similar receipt, but without plyr():

library(statnet)
net_summary <- function(net){

        size <- network.size(net)
        net_density <- gden(net)
        dyad_recip <- grecip(net)
        edge_recip <- grecip(net, measure="edgewise")
        trans <- gtrans(net)
        max_in <- max(api_indeg)
        max_out <- max(api_outdeg)
        max_clo <- max(api_clo)
        deg_centr <- centralization(net, degree, cmode="indegree")

        list("# of Nodes" = size,
             "Density" = net_density,
             "Max in-degree" = max_in,
             "Max out-degree" = max_out,
             "Degree centralization" = deg_centr,
             "Max betweenness" = max_bet,
             "Dyadic reciprocity" = dyad_recip,
             "Edgewise reciprocity" = edge_recip,
             "Transitivity" = trans)
}

net_summary_df <- sapply(networks, net_summary)
net_comparison <- as.data.frame(net_summary_df)

But I thought there is an easier and more natural way to add something to
statnet summary() function, because other SNA tools (ORA, NodeXL) show
basic things like density and reciprocity right away.

messages.body_plain:
Shupin,

I'm not sure that has been established for ergms yet.

In this case I would recommend using something like the rule of thumb for 
loglinear models, since you are fitting something similar to a multi-way 
table (at least 5 observations per cell) or the rule of thumb for logistic 
regressions (at least 10 "events" per predictor).  There's a good paper 
by Vittinghoff and McCullough on the latter here:
http://aje.oxfordjournals.org/content/165/6/710.full

The dependence across observations in network data make these rules of 
thumb for GLMs not directly comparable.

Perhaps someone else on the list has a better suggestion?

best,
mm

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm for weighted graphs
messages.body_plain:
Dear Giulia,

> I have a weighted network which is made of countries and the drug
> exchanges (estimated quantity) among them, and I would like to use an
> ergm to analyse it. I see from the workshop materials of the 2014
> Sunbelt that ergms for valued ties has been added in the list of
> additional functionalities. I have two questions about this:
> - Is there an updated tutorial on ergms for weighted graphs? (Or
> should I refer to the 2013 Sunbelt tutorial on valued networks? And,
> if so, is there any update since then?)

There is no updated tutorial, though we are planning to update it for
the 2016 Sunbelt. The 2013 tutorial is still valid, I think.

> - Do I need discrete data in my weighted network to run the ergm?

The ERGM terms designed for counts should also work reasonably well for
positive continuous measurements like what you have.

You can specify a continuous reference distribution by setting
reference=~Unif(a,b) where a and b are the minimum and the maximum
values or using reference=~StdNorm (with terms to model mean and
standard deviation --- let me know if you want more details), but
formulation and interpretation of these models has not yet been
explored.

In particular, if, in your data, there are 0s that are not just there
because the data are not available (missing), then the two references
above might not be appropriate. This is subject for ongoing work, but as
a stopgap, it might be appropriate to model such data conditionally: set
0s to NAs and fit a valued model using Unif or StdNorm, then fit a
binary ERGM for whether the value is 0 vs. nonzero (coded as 1).

                                                                   Sorry
I can't be more helpful,
                                                                   Pavel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Margaux,

It can't cope with NA values. There is a missing value for the dyad 
{B,C}. If you replace it with a non-negative real value, it works fine.

You may also want to use plot instead of gplot when you deal with 
network objects because it makes use of additional information like 
whether the network is directed (and thus omit the arrow heads 
automatically) etc.

Best,
Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Imputate missing edges with ERGM using an EM approach
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Imputate missing edges with ERGM using an EM approach
messages.body_plain:
Hi statnet users,

As part of my PhD, I'm working with a huge dynamical contact network 
(30s granularity, 600 nodes, ~6 months of data collection, roughly 3M 
edges in an undirected network). Ultimately, the idea is to study how 
dynamical processes influence the spread of nosocomial pathogens. The 
contact network was measured in a hospital and there is a clear 
clustering according to medical wards (5 in the dataset). Before doing 
anything about a spreading process, I'm trying to deal with missing 
data. I'm working with daily-aggregated networks for now, i.e. a set of 
daily edges between each pair of nodes. Although I could weight edges 
with daily-cumulative contact time, it's not really important right now.

All records were captured with individual sensors (meaning all 
participants wore a small wireless sensor at all time) that recorded the 
ID of other sensors in close proximity. Obviously some sensor batteries 
failed before others, and were not replaced until sheduled (there were 3 
interruptions in data collection on fixed date). Plotting the number of 
daily edges shows a tendency to decrease after batteries are replaced, 
which makes sense: therefore, the dataset is incomplete, with missing 
vertices (and edges going from/to them)... up until the next battery change.

i'm trying to implement an EM-like algorithm to impute missing edges, 
but so far it leads to degeneracy by leading to a graph with way more 
edges than I should expect (initially 1900 edges, 10% density ; ends at 
16000 edges ; 40% density). Here is the idea:
1) Initialize the network (let's call it nw) with all observed vertices 
and edges on day T.
2) From sensor attribution record, identify missing vertices from the 
network and add them (with add.vertices) along with a nodal attribute 
that keeps trace of them.
3) Fit an ERGM to nw, e.g.:
ergm.fit <- ergm(nw ~ edges + nodematch("affectation", diff=TRUE, 
keep=4:8) + nodematch("building", diff=T, keep=c(1,3)) + 
nodefactor("service") + nodecov("mif"))

NB: I have tried many of the higher-order structure ERGM termes (gwesp, 
gwdsp, altkstar) but couldn't really reproduce my observed graphs using 
them. However the ERGM I quote here is able to reproduce graphs that 
look a lot like the one I have observed in my dataset.

4) Simulate a new graph from the fit (call it nw.sim)
5) Extract the neighborhood of all vertices that have the "missing" 
attribute, and add these edges to the observed network nw
6) Repeat steps 4 and 5 until Beta estimates are stable enough between 
two iterations.


Here is the code I'm using:

nw.orig <- nw
converge <- FALSE
iter <- 1
trace <- list()
trace[[iter]] <- list(nw=nw.orig, ergm=ergm.fit)

while(!converge) {

   #Simulate from previous ERGM fit
   my.sim <- simulate(ergm.fit)

   #Extract new edges from missing vertices
   for (v in which(nw.orig %v% "missing")) {
     #cat(match(v, which(nw.orig %v% "missing")), "/", 
length(which(nw.orig %v% "missing")), "\n", sep="")
     v.neighbors <- get.neighborhood(my.sim, v=v)
     if (iter > 1) v.neighbors <- setdiff(v.neighbors, 
get.neighborhood(trace[[iter-1]]$nw, v=v))

     #Add them to the original network
     add.edges(nw, head=rep(v, length(v.neighbors)), tail=v.neighbors)
   }
   ergm.fit <- ergm(nw ~ edges + nodematch("affectation", diff=TRUE, 
keep=4:8) + nodematch("building", diff=T, keep=c(1,3)) + 
nodefactor("service") + nodecov("mif"))
   trace[[iter+1]] <- list(nw=nw, ergm=ergm.fit)
   plot(trace[[iter]]$ergm$coef - ergm.fit$coef, main=paste0("Iteration 
", iter))

   #Is convergency reached ? Obviously the threshold is too high, but 
for testing purposes ATM
   conv <- trace[[iter]]$ergm$coef - ergm.fit$coef
   if (!(any(conv > 0.1))) converge <- TRUE

   #Failsafe...
   if (iter > 100) break
   iter <- iter+1
}



I am wondering if this approach is correct. Maybe I should constrain 
fits to graphs that have the same density as the observed ones ? Offset 
the edges term ? I think degeneracy has to do with the terms in the ERGM 
being dependant on the number of edges, which is increasing from an 
iteration to the next.

I have another unrelated question, about ST-ERGMs. Are they in any way 
suitable to use with this kind of data (see first paragraph with a quick 
description of the dynamical network), to simulate formation and 
dissolution of edges ? Daily-aggregated networks are already a 
compressed version of the network, with time consistency not being kept, 
and I'm wondering how discretization might affect a spreading process. 
But fitting an ST-ERGM to such a big dataset... maybe not a good idea ?

Any help will be appreciated, and I hope I was clear enough!
Regards,
Thomas
